options.text: The tree is balanced, because the keys are placed one after another
options.explanation: Each key is larger than every key before it, so it always goes right: a chain, not a balanced tree.

options.text: Search stays O(log n), because a BST always halves the search space
options.explanation: A BST only halves the search space when it is balanced. This one is a chain, so each comparison rules out one key.

options.text: The tree becomes a chain of height 5, so finding 30 takes 6 comparisons: in the worst case, search is O(n)
options.explanation: Right. Each key is larger than all the keys before it, so each one goes right.

options.text: The height is 6, because there are 6 nodes
options.explanation: Height counts edges, not nodes. A chain of 6 nodes has height 5.

questions.stem: How does an AVL tree keep search fast?
questions.hint: This checks that you can explain what an AVL tree guarantees: rebalancing keeps the height, and so the search path, short.

options.text: It sorts the keys before inserting them
options.explanation: Sorting first would need extra work every time a key is added. An AVL tree restores balance with rotations instead.

options.text: Its search uses the balance factors to choose a shorter path
options.explanation: Search never reads balance factors. Balance helps because it limits how long any path can be.

options.text: It keeps every level completely full
options.explanation: An AVL tree does not have to be full. Branch heights may differ by 1 at any node.

options.text: After every insertion it checks balance factors and rotates where needed, so its height stays O(log n) and a search needs at most height + 1 comparisons
options.explanation: Right. Balance keeps the tree short, and a short tree means a short search path.

questions.stem: Which application suits an AVL tree best?
questions.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: A queue of print jobs, handled in the order they arrive
options.explanation: Jobs are never searched by key, and arrival order is all that matters: a queue is simpler.

options.text: A library catalogue: books are added during the day, staff search by ISBN thousands of times a day, and a list in ISBN order is printed each week
options.explanation: Right. Frequent searches by key, plus sorted output, is exactly what an AVL tree is good at.

options.text: A list of 10 high scores, rewritten once a day
options.explanation: With 10 items rarely searched, the balancing work buys nothing. A simple list is enough.

questions.stem: Student numbers arrive in increasing order as students register, and they are looked up often. Why is an AVL tree a better choice than a plain BST here?
questions.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: An AVL tree uses less memory than a plain BST
options.explanation: It uses more: each node stores its height. The benefit is guaranteed fast search.

options.text: Increasing numbers would make a plain BST a chain with O(n) search; the AVL tree rebalances after each insertion, so search stays O(log n)
options.explanation: Right. The sorted arrival order is the worst case for a plain BST.

options.text: AVL insertion is faster than plain BST insertion
options.explanation: AVL insertion does extra work (updating balance factors, rotating). The payoff is fast search.

options.text: AVL search uses the balance factors to find student numbers faster
options.explanation: Search reads only the keys. Balance helps by keeping the tree short.

questions.stem: Which application suits an AVL tree best?
questions.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: A queue of customers, served in arrival order
options.explanation: Customers are never searched by key; a queue fits.

options.text: A temporary list of 5 items that is printed once and thrown away
options.explanation: Too small and short-lived for balancing to pay off.

options.text: A phone’s contacts list: searched many times a day and always shown in alphabetical order
options.explanation: Right. Frequent search plus sorted order.

questions.stem: A shop has 50,000 product codes. Codes are looked up at every sale, a price list sorted by code is printed weekly, and new products are added a few times a day. Which structure fits best?
questions.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: An AVL tree keyed on product code
options.explanation: Right. Lookups dominate, the data must be listed in order, and updates are rare.

options.text: An unsorted list, because new products are added often
options.explanation: A few additions a day is rare compared with a lookup at every sale, and an unsorted list makes each lookup O(n).

options.text: A plain BST, because product codes always arrive in random order
options.explanation: New codes are often issued in increasing order, which would turn a plain BST into a chain.

questions.stem: A dictionary app loads its words from a file sorted A to Z. Why is an AVL tree better than a plain BST here?
questions.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: The sorted file would build a plain BST into a chain with O(n) search; the AVL tree rebalances as words are inserted, so lookups stay O(log n)
options.explanation: Right.

options.text: An AVL tree stores the words in less memory
options.explanation: It stores a height in every node, so it uses slightly more.

options.text: AVL search skips nodes by using the balance factors
options.explanation: Search compares keys only.

questions.stem: What is the main cost of choosing an AVL tree instead of a plain BST?
questions.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: Searches become slower, because balance factors must be checked
options.explanation: Search ignores balance factors, so it is not slowed down.

options.text: Every node stores a height, and insertions and deletions do extra work to update balance factors and rotate
options.explanation: Right. That is the time and space trade-off for guaranteed O(log n) search.

options.text: There is no extra cost
options.explanation: Balance has a price on updates and in memory.

questions.stem: When can a plain BST be good enough instead of an AVL tree?
questions.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: When keys arrive in sorted order
options.explanation: Sorted order is the worst case: a chain.

options.text: When the system must guarantee O(log n) search in the worst case
options.explanation: Only a balanced tree gives that guarantee.

options.text: When it is built once from keys in random order and then only searched
options.explanation: Right. Random insertion order usually gives a bushy tree, though there is no guarantee.
